text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Wednesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Temporary staff are replacing permanent employees more and more. The number of people working short periods of time has more than doubled from 39,000 in 1990 to 87,200 last year, figures from Statistics Sweden show.

- For 10 days a private Swedish-Norwegian diving team will search central Stockholm waters for the gun that killed former Swedish Prime Minister Olof Palme. The group will use an ultrasound technique previously not used in Sweden. Although Swedish police will not be involved with the team, they say they will investigate any promising finds produced by the search.

- This year's catalogue from furniture store IKEA, which will soon be distributed to millions of Swedish homes, shows furnishings directed at the child-friendly household and has reduced prices on many items.
- More and more hospitals are suffering because of savings on health care. Hospitals are overcrowded and emergency treatment is inadequate.
- A campaign to reduce prices on train fares this summer has been successful. Passenger volumes rose 20 percent this summer compared to last year.

- Swedish newspapers made a loss of 15.8 million crowns in 1996, not including the 400 million crowns in state support. Revenue from advertising declined for most newspapers last year, which is the most important source of income.
- Drinks giant PepsiCo's decision to break its cooperation with Spendrups from 2001 came as a complete surprise to the Swedish drinks company. PepsiCo is to link forces with Pripps Ringnes instead.

- Rumours say Scandinavian Equity Partners (SEP), controlled by the Swedish business family the Wallenbergs, reached an agreement to buy cable television company Star TV from Singapore Telecom, which serves 230,000 Stockholm households. Swedish telecoms company Netcom also says it had an oral agreement to buy Star TV which is valued at an estimated 500,000 million to one billion crowns.

- A stronger dollar against the Swedish crown should benefit export firms such as Swedish telecoms group Ericsson and Swedish forestry companies. The dollar climbed above eight crowns for the first time since 1993 last week.

- Ericsson mobile telephone sales were much higher than Finnish rival Nokia's in the second quarter. Ericsson reported sales growth of 102 percent in the first half of 1997 compared to Nokia's 53 percent growth.
- Swedish vehicle maker Volvo is negotiating a bus contract in Australia worth around 1.1 billion crowns from the Sydney Transport Authority. The deal will be decided in the next few weeks.

- Lower sales prices and higher investments were behind a fall in six-month earnings for Swedish forestry company Stora . The company posted a profit after financial items of 1.22 billion crowns -- slightly above market expectations of 1.13 billion -- and net sales of 22.02 billion crowns against 24.04 billion a year earlier.

- Saab Automobile, which posted a pretax loss of 600 million crowns for the six month period against a loss of 428 million a year earlier, is expected to show a loss for the year nearing 1.5 billion crowns. The company said costs were partly because of marketing expenditure to make the brand name better known. The company is selling more cars, however.
